chunks: 1. Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Ubayd ibn Zur'arah said:
I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who fell upon a man and killed him, so he said: There is no liability upon him.
2. Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad from Al-Wasshash from Aban ibn Uthman from Ubayd ibn Zur'arah said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who fell upon a man from above the house, and one of them died, he said: There is no liability upon the upper one, and no liability upon the lower one.
3. Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Al-Husayn from Safwan ibn Yahya and Fadala from Al-Ala' from Muhammad ibn Muslim from one of them (peace be upon him):
Regarding a man who falls upon a man and kills him, he said: There is no liability upon him.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: The explanation in these narrations is that he is not liable if it was accidental due to slipping, but if someone pushed him, the liability is upon him, and he may seek compensation from the pusher.
4. What Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub narrated from Abdillah ibn Sinan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him):
Regarding a man who pushed a man onto another man and killed him, he said: The blood money is upon the one who fell upon the man, for the heirs of the deceased.
He said: And the one who was pushed may seek the blood money from the one who pushed him.
He said: And if the one who was pushed suffered any injury, it is also upon the pusher.
ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling on blood liability when one person falls on another causing death?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi compiles these narrations to clarify the distinction between *zaman* (accidental fall) and *dafa'* (active pushing) in Islamic jurisprudence, establishing that liability for *diyah* (blood money) rests on the active agent. The commentary by Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Wajih highlights that if the fall was due to a slip, there is no penalty, but if pushed, the victim of the push seeks compensation from the pusher, illustrating the principle of *'iqrar* (self-incrimination) and chain of causation in Shia legal theory.
